title: Anderson v. Binance
summary: The assigned 2026 opinion rejects Binance’s attempt to compel arbitration through later website terms, addressing both lack of constructive notice and the limits on retroactive modification.
notes:
This is a source-based account of the dated opinion in the course supplement. Subsequent proceedings and present legal status have not been checked. The omitted actual-notice analysis is identified as omitted rather than reconstructed.

Judge Andrew Carter (S.D.N.Y.) decided the motion on February 26, 2026; besides denying arbitration, the court held the class-action waiver in the 2019 Terms unenforceable against users who transacted under the 2017 Terms, because merely posting the revised terms on the website, with no evidence that the arbitration provision was announced, gave insufficient notice.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were users from California, Nevada, and Texas asserting securities claims after purchasing tokens on Binance. Binance and its founder sought to enforce an arbitration provision introduced after the users opened their accounts.
sections.Material Facts:
The users opened their accounts between September 2017 and April 2018 and undisputedly assented to the 2017 terms. Those terms lacked an arbitration clause, choice-of-law provision, and class-action waiver. A change-of-terms clause purported to allow amendments announced on the website without individual notice and treated continued use as acceptance. In February 2019 Binance posted new terms requiring Singapore arbitration and adding a Singapore choice-of-law clause.

Users continued using their accounts to different degrees. Binance provided no evidence of contemporaneous individual notice or an announcement meeting the original clause’s own terms. The record also did not show that users were told where to look for amendments. An editorial omission states that the court found actual notice by June 8, 2020. That later actual-notice conclusion must be distinguished from constructive notice at the time of the change and from retroactive application to accrued claims.
sections.Procedural History: The initial complaint was filed in 2020. After dismissal in 2022 and appellate reversal in 2024, plaintiffs filed a third amended complaint and defendants renewed their request to compel arbitration. The supplied February 26, 2026 district-court opinion denies that motion. It does not decide the merits of the securities claims.
sections.Issue: Could the later terms supply their own governing-law clause, did posting them establish assent under the original amendment clause, and could the arbitration requirement reach earlier accrued claims?
sections.Holding: The disputed 2019 choice-of-law clause could not determine its own adoption. The court found insufficient constructive notice of the amendment and separately concluded that the arbitration language could not retroactively govern claims accrued or known before its effective date. The motion to compel was denied.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first identified the state law applicable to the formation question without assuming the disputed clause was binding. It applied the laws of the users’ states, which the parties agreed produced the same relevant result. A valid initial clickwrap agreement did not automatically establish assent to every later website amendment. The court distinguished a banking case in which individual communications directed users to a previously agreed disclosure channel. Here the users had no equivalent reason to find the new provision.

The retroactivity analysis supplied a separate restriction. The court distinguished clauses expressly permitting opportunistic changes to known claims from clauses silent about temporal scope. It read the latter in light of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, restricting changes from reaching accrued or known claims. The decision therefore links assent to modification and the limits on contractual discretion. Later actual notice alone did not answer the separate question whether an amendment could govern already accrued claims.

textbookImport.basis: Paraphrase of the exact supplied Fall 2026 Contracts Supplement; no subsequent-treatment review.

learning.why: Although assigned in the unconscionability unit, the reproduced reasoning chiefly concerns assent, modification, choice of law, and good faith. It belongs in all of those indexes.

topics.assent: Initial agreement does not automatically prove acceptance of later website terms.
topics.modification: Examines notice and temporal limits on unilateral amendments.
topics.discretion: Limits a company’s reserved power to alter terms affecting accrued claims.
topics.good-faith: Uses the implied covenant to restrict silent amendment language.
topics.standard-forms: Compares initial clickwrap assent with later browsewrap amendment.
topics.governing-law: Declines to use a disputed choice-of-law provision to establish its own enforceability.
topics.notice: The decision turns on whether merely posting revised terms gives users constructive notice of an arbitration clause.
topics.arbitration-formation: Whether the 2019 arbitration clause bound users was treated as a contract-formation question decided under ordinary assent principles.
topics.adhesion: The change-of-terms clause in a standardized online agreement is the mechanism the court refused to let operate unilaterally.
